scenes.text: Almost every advanced chip on Earth is printed in one place.

The machine that prints the smallest circuits exists in a single version, built by one Dutch company. It fires a laser at molten tin droplets fifty thousand times a second to make light thirteen nanometers wide, and focuses it with mirrors so smooth that scaled to the size of a country, the tallest bump would be a millimeter. Almost all of the leading-edge output runs through Taiwan.

Strategists call this the silicon shield. The theory is that being indispensable is its own kind of armor. Nobody wrecks the factory the whole world depends on. But a shield and a target can be the same object viewed from two directions. And the deeper issue is quieter. We built the most complex supply chain in history and then stacked it on a single point of failure, because concentration was cheaper than redundancy.
